question: In Norway, a citizen was fined and threatened with prison for refusing a PCR test and quarantine hotel in 2021. After Norwegian courts declined to engage with her arguments, she has applied to the European Court of Human Rights1. Similar cases from EU Member States are also pending in Strasbourg, including challenges to vaccine mandates in France2, school closures in Germany3, and assembly restrictions in Croatia4.

These cases highlight a wider European issue: individuals are still facing prosecutions and penalties years after the pandemic, despite serious questions of proportionality, necessity, and compliance with fundamental rights. 1.

How does the Commission assess the compatibility of ongoing prosecutions and penalties linked to COVID-19 measures with the principles of necessity and proportionality under the Charter of Fundamental Rights?

While the Commission has evaluated EU health preparedness, it has not reviewed pandemic restrictions for proportionality and compliance with fundamental rights. Will it commit to launching a rights-focused review to prevent misuse of emergency powers in future crises?
In the context of its annual rule of law reports, how will the Commission ensure that the legacy of pandemic restrictions – including ongoing prosecutions – is addressed within this framework?

Granada v Norway, application reportedly lodged in 2024 (not yet available on the Human Rights Documentation (HUDOC) database at the time of writing; information based on applicant’s public statements). De Haro v France and Others, Nos 31119/22, 35013/22 and 35141/22, communicated on 16 May 2024, HUDOC. M.C.K. and M.H.K.-B. and Others v Germany, No 10975/21, communicated case, HUDOC. Magdić v Croatia, No 17578/20, communicated case, HUDOC.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.12.2025) The impact and challenges brought by the COVID-19 pandemic from a rule of law perspective have also been examined in the Commission’s Rule of Law reports. The Commission made clear from the outset that the response to the COVID-19 pandemic must fully respect the fundamental principles and values as set out in the Treaties.

Emergency measures had to be limited to what is necessary, strictly proportionate, clearly restricted in time, and in line with constitutionally enshrined safeguards, as well as European and international standards. The Commission has no competence to comment on individual cases. The Commission can only intervene with the Member States in the area of fundamental rights if an issue of EU law is involved1.

The organisation of and the delivery of healthcare services, such as COVID-19 testing, are the competence of EU Member States. In such cases, it is for Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected, in accordance with their national legislation and constitution, as well as their international human rights obligations.

Contrary to the statement in the question, the Commission and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control have reviewed pandemic restrictions for proportionality, effectiveness and social impact2.
